narrative_idea_gen: Presented as the "fully authenticated and unabridged" memoir of one Geraldine Fitch — sole survivor of what suburban historians now call the 1987 Cutlery Creek Block Party Massacre — this is the blood-soaked, breathlessly funny account of a sixty-one-year-old woman fleeing through a labyrinth of identical cul-de-sacs as her neighbor Dale Spurlock, a man driven to homicidal single-mindedness over seventeen years of unpaid HOA fence-height violations, pursues her with an escalating arsenal of hedge trimmers, decorative katanas, and a gas-powered edger. Geraldine — asthmatic, terrible with directions, and perpetually barefoot after losing her sandals in the Hendersons' koi pond — narrates her desperate, gore-slicked flight with the maddening digressiveness of a woman who cannot stop rating the landscaping of every yard she crawls through, even as she catalogues in queasy, visceral detail exactly what Dale's brush hook did to the Waterson twins' above-ground pool and everyone in it. The comedy is relentless and irresistible precisely because Geraldine understands she is prey, has *always* been prey since Dale first measured her fence in 1970, and her only resource is an encyclopedic knowledge of neighborhood gossip that lets her predict which unlocked back doors and secret affair-routes between houses might keep her one hedge-row ahead of a man who will not stop until every violation is corrected in blood.

# Seven Structural Beats for *The Cutlery Creek Block Party Massacre*

---

## Beat 1: The Authenticating Apparatus

**What to Build:** An editorial frame — footnotes, a foreword, an archivist's note, a publication history, or some combination — written in the dry, self-important register of suburban local historiography. This voice presents Geraldine's memoir as a recovered document. It authenticates, contextualizes, and subtly *contains* her account. It should mention Dale Spurlock's name with the clinical neutrality of a case file. It should mention the body count the way a municipal report mentions potholes. It should note, in passing, some small institutional detail — perhaps that the Cutlery Creek HOA was formally dissolved in 1988, or that Geraldine moved to a condo in Tucson and "declined further involvement in homeowner governance" — that sounds like a footnote but is actually a scream.

**Structural Function (adapted from Beat 1 of the reference):** *Frame narrative with register shift.* The editorial voice speaks in the dead language of institutions — the same bureaucratic infrastructure that produced Dale's seventeen years of fence-height grievances. Geraldine's memoir speaks in the living, digressive, ungovernable language of a woman who cannot stop *noticing things* even while running for her life. The shift between registers IS the argument. The HOA produces paperwork. Geraldine produces testimony. The system that enabled the massacre and the system that "authenticates" the memoir are the same system. They speak the same language. Geraldine does not.

**Why It Matters:** The frame must do what Lu Xun's preface does: deliver the most devastating piece of information before the reader knows it's devastating. If the frame tells us Geraldine is the *sole survivor*, then every neighbor she subsequently mentions by name — every yard she rates, every koi pond she catalogues, every affair-route she knows — belongs to a dead person. The reader will not feel this on first encounter. But as the memoir proceeds, the frame's bland "sole survivor" will retroactively become the worst sentence in the document. The frame also pre-cancels Geraldine's survival as a victory: she lived, moved to a condo, and the HOA was dissolved, which sounds like resolution. It is not. She survived by knowing which doors were unlocked because of whose husband was sleeping with whom. She *survived by gossip.* The system that saved her is the same system that rotted the neighborhood from within. The frame should make "declined further involvement in homeowner governance" sound exactly the way "recovered and took a government post" sounds in Lu Xun: like a person who stopped screaming because screaming changed nothing.

---

## Beat 2: The Fence Measurement, 1970

**What to Build:** Geraldine's account of the *first* time Dale Spurlock measured her fence. This should be a memory nested inside the present-tense flight — she is already running, already barefoot, already bleeding from the koi pond — but she cannot help beginning at the beginning, because Geraldine is a woman who believes in *context.* The memory should be banal to the point of comedy: Dale with a tape measure, Dale in pleated shorts, Dale not making eye contact but staring at the fence with a focus that, at the time, she found merely annoying. The detail that makes it sinister must be small and domestic: perhaps the way he wrote the measurement down in a pocket notebook, or the way he didn't respond when she said good morning, or the way the tape measure snapped back into its housing with a sound she can still hear seventeen years later.

**Structural Function (adapted from Beat 2 of the reference):** *The mundane object as origin of all horror.* The tape measure is the Zhao family's dog. It is specific, domestic, ridiculous, and therefore impossible to dismiss. The technique is juxtaposition without transition: 1970, Dale measures a fence, Geraldine thinks nothing of it. 1987, Dale measures the neighborhood in blood. The reader must feel both timelines simultaneously. The comedy comes from the disproportion — a man slaughtering people over *fence height* — but the horror comes from the fact that Geraldine herself identifies the exact moment threat entered her world and she *did not recognize it.* She sensed something in the way the dog — the neighbor — looked at her. She filed it away as an eccentricity. Every suburban reader has done the same. The gap between "odd neighbor" and "homicidal neighbor" must be kept razor-thin, because in real neighborhoods it *is* razor-thin, and that is the joke, and that is the terror.

**Why It Matters:** This beat establishes the temporal architecture of the whole memoir. Geraldine narrates in two timescales — the crawl-by-crawl flight through the cul-de-sac (minutes, hours) and the seventeen-year accumulation of HOA grievances (the backstory she can't stop providing). The fence measurement in 1970 is the founding trauma she didn't know was a trauma. It must feel, on first read, like a comic digression — Geraldine, you are *fleeing for your life*, why are you telling us about pleated shorts in 1970? — and on second read, like the most important paragraph in the book. Everything Dale does tonight was authored in that moment. Geraldine knows this. That is why she begins here, even though she is bleeding. She is not digressing. She is testifying.

---

## Beat 3: The First Yard, the First Body, the First Landscaping Review

**What to Build:** Geraldine, mid-flight, crawls through the first neighbor's yard — and gives us, in unbroken narration, three things simultaneously: (a) a visceral, physically specific account of what Dale has done to someone, (b) a running critique of the yard's landscaping, mulch choices, or lawn hydration, and (c) a piece of neighborhood gossip about the people who lived here that is both completely irrelevant to survival and absolutely essential to the portrait of Cutlery Creek. These three streams must be genuinely *braided*, not alternating. Geraldine does not pause the horror for comedy or pause the comedy for horror. She does them in the same sentence because *she is the kind of person who does them in the same sentence.* This is the beat that teaches the reader how to read the rest of the book.

**Structural Function (adapted from Beat 3 of the reference):** *Escalation through category violation.* The reference story escalates by moving from adults to children — from expected hostility to innocence conscripted into the system. Here, the category violation is *Geraldine's own narration.* A normal narrator would describe flight and violence. Geraldine describes flight, violence, *and* whether the Hendersons' hostas are properly spaced. The violation is tonal: the reader expects the horror to silence the trivia, or the trivia to defuse the horror. Neither happens. The two coexist without hierarchy. This is not comic relief. This is a woman whose entire cognitive apparatus — the thing that makes her *her* — cannot turn off, even in extremis. The horror is that the world is ending and Geraldine's mind is still filing HOA observations. The deeper horror is that those observations are what will save her life, because knowing which yard has a broken gate latch and which yard has a compost pile tall enough to hide behind *is* a form of survival knowledge. The system colonized Geraldine's mind with landscaping minutiae and gossip, and that colonization is now, grotesquely, her only weapon. The reader must laugh. The reader must also feel the vertigo of recognizing that Geraldine's "digressiveness" is actually *total situational awareness* expressed in the only language she has.

**Why It Matters:** This is where the reader either bonds with Geraldine permanently or doesn't. The gamble is that her voice — her inability to stop *rating things*, her insistence on social context in a slaughterhouse — will be so specific and so relentless that the reader cannot help loving her even as they want to shake her. The comedy must be *irresistible* (the reference brief's word, and the right one). It must also accumulate a body count. Every yard is a dead neighbor. Every landscaping review is an inadvertent eulogy. The reader should realize, several yards in, that Geraldine is memorializing these people the only way she knows how: by remembering what their yards looked like, what their secrets were, what they cared about. Her digressions are grief. She just doesn't know how to grieve any other way.

---

## Beat 4: The Gossip Map — Reading the Neighborhood Between the Lines

**What to Build:** A set piece — perhaps while Geraldine is hiding in a shed, a garage, a half-built gazebo — in which she explicates, in rapid-fire detail, the social geography of Cutlery Creek. Who is sleeping with whom. Who has a key to whose back door and *why.* Which property line disputes were actually proxy wars for older resentments. Which family's Christmas decorations were a coded insult to which other family. The gossip should be *staggeringly* comprehensive, delivered with the authority of a tenured anthropologist, and it should constitute, without Geraldine ever naming it as such, a complete *tactical map* of her escape route. She knows which doors are unlocked because she knows which affairs are active. She knows which fences have loose boards because she knows which feuds resulted in sabotage. Her gossip is intelligence. Her nosiness is survival.

**Structural Function (adapted from Beat 4 of the reference):** *The palimpsest reading, transposed.* In the reference, the madman reads a history book and sees "eat people" between every line. Here, Geraldine reads *the neighborhood itself* — its architecture, its social rituals, its landscaping — and sees between every line the truth that polite suburbia labors to conceal: that every house is a node in a web of desire, resentment, secrecy, and petty territorial violence that has been operating for decades and of which Dale's massacre is merely the *most literal expression.* The technique converts gossip — the most dismissed, feminized, "trivial" form of knowledge — into a life-saving hermeneutic. Geraldine reads the neighborhood the way the madman reads the history book: obsessively, associatively, and with results that look like paranoia but function as revelation.

**Why It Matters:** This is the mirror of Beat 4 in the reference — the moment the reader is forced to perform the same act of interpretation as the narrator. The reader of Geraldine's memoir is *doing what Geraldine does:* reading between the surface of suburban domestic life and finding the hidden networks of transgression. If you enjoy the gossip (and you will, because Geraldine is very good at gossip), you are participating in the same surveillance apparatus that Geraldine has internalized. The reader's pleasure in learning who was sleeping with whom is *complicity* with the neighborhood's own obsessive regulation of private behavior — the same regulation that, pushed to its psychotic endpoint, produced Dale and his tape measure and his brush hook. The form enacts the content. Gossip saves Geraldine. Gossip also *is* the low-grade suburban panopticon that made Dale possible. The reader should feel both truths simultaneously and not be able to separate them.

---

## Beat 5: Dale's Grievance File — The HOA as the Enabling Architecture

**What to Build:** A beat — perhaps found by Geraldine mid-flight, or perhaps recalled from years of HOA meetings — in which the full bureaucratic record of Dale's fence-height complaints is laid bare. Seventeen years of properly filed violation reports. Minutes from meetings at which Dale raised the issue and was *heard*, technically, but dismissed, redirected, tabled. Letters from the HOA board acknowledging receipt of his complaints. Perhaps a form letter — boilerplate, form-number and all — thanking Mr. Spurlock for his "continued commitment to community standards." The documents should be real in texture: the passive voice, the cc'd parties, the action items that lead to no action. They should be both darkly funny and genuinely chilling, because they reveal that the system *processed Dale perfectly.* It received his rage in measured increments, validated it with form letters, and never once asked why a man had spent seventeen years measuring the same fence. The HOA did not ignore Dale. It *administered* him.

**Structural Function (adapted from Beat 5 of the reference):** *The institution as the elder brother.* In the reference, the elder brother is the patriarchal authority who arranges the doctor's visit — the system wearing a family face, the violence administered through care. Here, the HOA is the elder brother. It is the structure that domesticated Dale's obsession, gave it a procedural vocabulary, provided it a venue (the meeting, the form, the violation code), and thereby *legitimized the framework of measurement and enforcement* that Dale eventually carried to its logical conclusion. Dale is not an aberration of the HOA. He is its most faithful adherent. Every line of the HOA's boilerplate is double-coded: "We appreciate your attention to community standards" is both bureaucratic pleasantry and inadvertent commissioning of a massacre. narrative_story:
# The Cutlery Creek Block Party Massacre

## Being the Complete and Unabridged Personal Account of Mrs. Geraldine Mosby (née Yates), Sole Surviving Resident of Cutlery Creek Estates, Regarding the Events of June 13, 1987

---

**Editor's Note**

The following document was recovered in 2019 from the personal effects of Mrs. Geraldine Anne Mosby (1932–2018) following her death at the Sunrise Palms condominium complex in Tucson, Arizona. Mrs. Mosby had lived at Sunrise Palms since relocating from the Dayton, Ohio, metropolitan area in late 1987.¹ The manuscript, handwritten in blue ballpoint on seventy-three sheets of yellow legal pad paper, appears to have been composed in a concentrated period between September and November of 1987, approximately three to five months after the events described. Several pages bear water stains consistent with glass rings. One page (here designated p. 47) contains a marginal drawing of what appears to be a bird feeder, rendered in considerable detail, beside a paragraph describing the death of Margaret Ohlsen.

The text is presented here without significant editorial alteration, though obvious misspellings have been silently corrected and Mrs. Mosby's occasionally idiosyncratic punctuation has been standardized for readability. Her paragraph breaks, such as they are, have been preserved. Her underlinings — which are frequent, emphatic, and rarely predictable in their targets — have been rendered in italics.

For context: The Cutlery Creek Estates subdivision was a planned residential community of forty-six single-family homes located approximately eleven miles southeast of central Dayton, in unincorporated Greene County. Developed in 1968 by Prestige Home Corporation (later Prestige-National, later defunct), the subdivision was governed from its inception by a homeowners association whose bylaws, adopted in 1969, included provisions for architectural review, common-area maintenance, and the enforcement of residential standards including but not limited to fence height, lawn maintenance, exterior paint color, and the permissibility of various ornamental features.² The HOA was formally dissolved by unanimous vote of its four surviving non-resident property holders on February 3, 1988.

On the evening of June 13, 1987, during the subdivision's annual block party, resident Dale Edward Spurlock (1934–1987) killed twenty-seven people over a period of approximately ninety minutes using a brush hook, a gasoline-powered hedge trimmer, and a Ball-Peen hammer.³ Spurlock was found deceased the following morning on the median strip of Cutlery Creek Drive by officers of the Greene County Sheriff's Department.⁴ Mrs. Mosby was the sole surviving resident present at the event.

Mrs. Mosby was contacted by the Greene County Historical Preservation Society in 1994, 1997, and 2003 regarding the possible donation of her manuscript to the county archive. She declined on each occasion. In her final response, dated November 11, 2003, she wrote: "I have received your letter and I appreciate the interest. I would prefer not to. I am no longer involved in any form of homeowner governance and I would like to continue not being involved in any form of homeowner governance. The bird feeders here are adequate."

We are grateful to Mrs. Mosby's niece, Sandra Mosby-Kline, for permission to publish.

— *Dr. Janet Hoch, Department of Local and Regional History, Wright State University*  
— *Kevin Brill, M.A., Greene County Historical Preservation Society*

April 2020

---

¹ Property records indicate Mrs. Mosby purchased Unit 14-C at Sunrise Palms on October 2, 1987, in a cash transaction. She does not appear to have returned to Ohio.

² A complete set of Cutlery Creek Estates HOA bylaws, meeting minutes (1969–1987), and associated correspondence is held in the Greene County Clerk's Office, File No. 88-CR-4412, Exhibit Binders 7 through 19. The collection runs to approximately 2,400 pages. Mr. Spurlock is the author or subject of an estimated 340 of those pages.

³ The brush hook, a long-handled agricultural cutting tool, was identified as the primary weapon. It was recovered from the front lawn of 14 Cutlery Creek Drive. The hedge trimmer, a Stihl model HS-76, was recovered from the pool area of the subdivision's common lot, where it had apparently run out of fuel. The hammer was found in Mr. Spurlock's right hand.

⁴ The county coroner's report attributed Mr. Spurlock's death to a self-inflicted incision. A handwritten note was found in his shirt pocket reading, in its entirety: "SEE ATTACHED VIOLATIONS." No attachment was recovered.

---

## The Account of Geraldine Mosby

I want to say first off that Barbara Ridley's agapanthus was not properly mulched and never had been, not in any of the years I lived across the street from her, and whatever else happened that night, this fact should be entered into the record because I tried to bring it up at the meeting in April and Hal Westbrook talked right over me the way he always did when he thought a woman was being *particular,* and then three months later a man with a brush hook came through the cul-de-sac like God's own weed-whacker and it turned out being particular was the only thing that saved my life, so perhaps Hal should have listened, though of course by the time he might have reconsidered the value of listening he was in the Ridley pool and not in a swimming capacity.

I am writing this in Tucson because there is nowhere else to write it. The condo has adequate light. The bird feeders attract a type of hummingbird that Sandra tells me is called Anna's hummingbird and one that I believe is a Rufous, though the Rufous may be a different bird visiting at odd hours. I have no one to consult on this because I no longer know my neighbors and I intend to continue not knowing my neighbors for the remainder of my natural life, however long that turns out to be, which given the family history and the fact that I am eating better out here — the grapefruit situation is *outrageously* good — may be considerable.

But I have to go back.

I want to set the context.

People will say Dale just snapped, and I want to say first that a man does not *snap.* A man does what a man has been practicing in miniature for decades, and Dale Spurlock had been practicing his particular form of measurement since at least 1970, which is when he first came to my fence with a tape measure and I learned something about him that I filed away in the part of my brain where I keep things I have noticed but cannot yet *use,* the way you keep a button in a drawer because you don't know which coat it fell off of but you know it fell off of *something.*

---

It was a Tuesday. I know it was a Tuesday because I had just gotten back from the Kroger on Dorothy Lane, which I only went to on Tuesdays because Wednesdays were when Connie Ferris went and Connie Ferris had a habit of standing in the cereal aisle and telling you about her son's orthodontic situation for a duration that could not be measured with any instrument known to modern science, and I say this as a woman who has just spent an evening crawling through a neighborhood with a man who took measurement *very seriously,* so I feel I am qualified to speak on the limits of measurement.

I was putting the groceries away. I had purchased a reasonable quantity of canned pears — the Dole ones in light syrup, not the Del Monte, because the Del Monte packed in heavy syrup and heavy syrup on a canned pear is an act of aggression against the pear — and I was stacking these in the pantry when I saw, through the kitchen window, Dale Spurlock standing at my side fence with a tape measure.

Now.

I should describe Dale Spurlock for posterity.

Dale was not a large man or a small man. He was the exact size you would expect of a man who would one day kill twenty-seven people at a block party with a brush hook, which is to say he was *medium.* He was of medium height and medium build and he wore pleated khaki shorts that were exactly the color of *institutional disappointment,* a sort of beige that gave up on itself halfway through the dyeing process. He had a short-sleeve button-down shirt — also beige, also defeated — and white tennis shoes of the kind that were sold at Sears and purchased by men who had never played tennis and did not intend to start. He had a pocket protector. He had a pocket protector in 1970 and he had a pocket protector in 1987 and I am certain that if the coroner's office checked, they would find that he died with a pocket protector, because Dale Spurlock did not enter any situation without preparation for the taking of notes.

He was standing at my fence — which was a four-foot painted cedar fence, regulation height, I want to be very clear about this, it was *four feet* — and he had the tape measure extended from the ground to the top rail, and he was looking at the tape measure the way a doctor looks at an X-ray. Not at the fence. Not at the yard. Not at me, standing in my own kitchen in my own house on a Tuesday with canned pears in my hands. At the *measurement.* The number on the tape was the only living thing in his field of vision.

I went outside. This was 1970. You went outside when a neighbor was at your fence. You did not call anyone. You went out and you said good morning and you asked if everything was all right and this was the social contract and this was what the brochure from Prestige Home Corporation had sold us on when Gerald and I bought the lot in 1968: *community.* Neighbors who looked out for each other. Neighbors who *noticed.*

I said, "Good morning, Dale."

He did not look up.

I said it again. "Good morning."

He wrote a number in a pocket notebook — a small spiral one, the kind reporters used on television shows — and then he pressed the button on the tape measure and it retracted. The sound it made was a snap and a hiss together. Like a small animal biting its own tail. I can hear it right now, sitting in Tucson with the hummingbirds, I can hear the exact pitch and duration of that tape measure retracting, which is a terrible thing to carry in your head for seventeen years but I have carried worse since June and I believe I will carry worse still before the Rufous and I are done.

Then he looked at me.

He had colorless eyes. I don't mean they were pale blue or light grey. I mean they were the color of *nothing.* They were the color of the space between channels on a television set. He looked at me and he did not greet me and he said — and this was the only thing he said, and this was the thing I put in the drawer with the button — he said: "Four feet and one-quarter inch."

Then he left.

I stood in my yard with the smell of cut grass and the sound of the Hendersons' sprinkler system going *tch-tch-tch-tch* and I thought: *That's a strange man.* And then I went back inside and I finished putting away the canned pears and I started the laundry and I did not think about Dale Spurlock again for several weeks, at which point the first HOA violation notice arrived in our mailbox, typed on a manual typewriter, citing Cutlery Creek Estates Bylaws Section 4, Subsection 2(a), regarding the maximum permissible fence height of forty-eight inches, accompanied by a handwritten note in the margin that read: "48.25 inches. See measurement. Attached."

Gerald laughed. Gerald was alive then and inclined to laugh at things that later turned out not to be funny, which was his primary quality as a husband and I loved him for it and I occasionally wanted to strangle him for it, which is I suppose the range available in a marriage. He said, "Gerry, the man measured your fence and you're a quarter inch over. That's just Dale. That's just *Dale being Dale.*"

That was the phrase people used. That was the phrase the whole neighborhood used for seventeen years. *Dale being Dale.* Dale measuring the Ohlsens' mailbox post and finding it two inches too close to the sidewalk. Dale photographing the Chens' Christmas lights and submitting a formal complaint that the icicle-style lights constituted a "non-approved hanging ornamental feature." Dale at every single HOA meeting with his spiral notebook and his pocket protector and his colorless eyes, raising his hand during the open comment period and reading, in a voice that was the audio equivalent of his beige shorts, a prepared statement about setback violations and drainage-grade interference and the ongoing, *unconscionable* non-compliance of multiple residents with the fence-height provisions of Section 4, Subsection 2(a).

Dale being Dale.

And every time he did it, and every time the board thanked him for his input and tabled the matter and moved on to the question of whether to resurface the tennis court, something in Dale's colorless eyes did not go away. It *accumulated.* It was there at the next meeting and the next and the next, and it was a quarter-inch thicker each time, like sediment, like something geological, and I saw it and I filed it and I told Gerald once, in 1978, "That man is going to do something one day," and Gerald said, "He's going to do something all right, he's going to bore us all to death," and then Gerald laughed the laugh of a man who was not, as it turned out, going to die of boredom.

Gerald died of a heart attack in 1983, in the driveway, carrying a bag of mulch. Cedar mulch. I had asked him to buy cypress but they were out. That is the kind of detail I cannot stop providing and I want to acknowledge that I am aware of it as a tendency and I do not intend to curb it because these details are the only things I have left and I will hold them with both hands until my hands stop working.

---

The night of June 13, 1987, I was at the block party, which was held annually in the cul-de-sac at the end of Cutlery Creek Drive. There was a potluck arrangement. Connie Ferris brought her corn casserole, which tasted the way her son's orthodontic stories felt: like something endured rather than enjoyed. The Hendersons brought bratwurst. Barbara Ridley brought a fruit salad with Cool Whip that she called "ambrosia" the way Napoleon called himself Emperor — with complete conviction and no supporting evidence.

I had brought deviled eggs, which were good, because I am good at deviled eggs, and I do not say this to boast but to *record,* because those were the last deviled eggs I made for a neighborhood function and I want it known they were well-received.

Dale was not at the block party. Dale was never at the block party. Dale had not attended a social function in Cutlery Creek Estates since 1979, when he came to the Hendersons' Fourth of July picnic and spent the entire event measuring the setback between the Hendersons' portable badminton net and the property line. This was the year Joan Henderson asked him to leave, and he left, and he did not come back to any gathering, and no one thought this was a problem because Dale not being at a party was the best thing that could happen to a party, which is a horrible thing to say about a person and is also true and I am finished pretending those two things cannot both be true at the same time.

At approximately 7:40 in the evening — and I know the time because I had just looked at my watch to calculate whether I could leave by 8:00 without being rude, which was a calculation I performed at every neighborhood event with the precision Dale brought to fence measurement — the first thing I heard was not a scream.
